failures.title: Audi CPMA Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Timing Chain Tensioner Wear - 2012-2015 models
items.whatHappens: The rear-mounted timing chain tensioner in this generation of 3.0 TDI can lose pressure over time, leading to chain stretch. This manifests as a distinct cold-start rattle from the rear of the engine. If ignored, the chain can skip a tooth, causing catastrophic valve-to-piston contact.
items.repairVsReplace: A standalone timing chain kit replacement is labour-intensive due to rear access but is a viable repair (£1,500-£2,500). However, if the chain has already jumped or caused internal damage, a full Audi CPMA engine replacement becomes the only reliable solution. Read our full timing chain failure guide.

items.title: EGR Cooler and Oil Cooler Leaks
items.whatHappens: The EGR cooler and oil cooler are prone to internal seal degradation. This can lead to coolant mixing with engine oil (creating a milky sludge) or external leaks that drip onto the turbocharger and exhaust components, posing a fire risk and causing overheating.
items.repairVsReplace: Replacing the EGR and oil cooler assemblies is the standard repair. If coolant contamination has severely degraded the engine bearings, a reconditioned CPMA engine is often more cost-effective than a bottom-end rebuild. Read our full EGR cooler failure guide.

failures.goodYearsLine: Post-2015 CPMA units received revised timing chain tensioners and updated EGR cooler designs, significantly reducing the incidence of these specific failures .

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the CPMA
variants.intro: The Audi CPMA engine code is stamped directly onto the engine block, typically on a machined pad near the junction of the engine and the transmission bell housing. It is also clearly listed on your V5C registration document under "Engine Number" and can be decoded from your 17-digit VIN.

relatives.description: - The earlier 3.0 TDI V6 that preceded the CPMA, sharing the same fundamental architecture but lacking the refined Euro 6 emissions hardware and updated timing chain tensioners.
- The updated 3.0 TDI variant that succeeded the CPMA, featuring further refined AdBlue dosing software and improved EGR cooler durability.

The CPMA architecture is genuinely shared across the wider Volkswagen Group, meaning the physical engine block and internal components are virtually identical to those found in the and 3.0 TDI models of the same era.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement Audi CPMA - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used Audi CPMA engine is a viable option only if it comes with a verifiable service history proving regular oil changes and a recent timing chain tensioner update. Without this documentation, you risk inheriting hidden chain stretch or EGR cooler leaks that will trigger failures shortly after installation. Explore vetted options via our used engines network.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A properly reconditioned CPMA is the recommended choice for most owners. A reputable rebuild will include a revised timing chain tensioner, new EGR and oil cooler assemblies, and a verified turbocharger, directly addressing the 3.0 TDI V6's known weak points and restoring the engine to near-factory reliability. Compare reconditioned engines today.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for high-mileage CPMA units that have suffered secondary damage, such as a jumped timing chain leading to valve damage, or severe coolant contamination destroying the main bearings. An upgraded rebuild should include line-boring the block and fitting new piston rings to restore factory compression. Learn more about rebuilt engines.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Opting for a supply-and-fit service through our network ensures the replacement is performed by Audi specialists, with the warranty backed by the installing garage for complete peace of mind. View our supply and fit options.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The CPMA is typically found in Audi A6 C7, A7 C7, and Q7 4L/4M models valued between £6,000 and £25,000 . For lower-value examples (sub-£8,000), a reconditioned engine costing £3,500+ may approach 50% of the vehicle's current market value. If the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate scrap value before committing.

mainEntity.name: How much does an Audi CPMA engine replacement cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A reconditioned Audi CPMA engine typically costs between £3,500 and £5,500 for supply-only . Used units start around £1,500 but carry high risks of undocumented timing chain wear. Fully rebuilt options range from £5,000 to £7,500. Independent fitting labour adds approximately £780-£1,040 to the total.

mainEntity.name: What is the most common failure with the CPMA engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most frequent documented issue with the Audi CPMA is timing chain tensioner wear, often accompanied by EGR cooler leaks. The rear-mounted tensioner can lose pressure, leading to chain stretch and a distinct cold-start rattle. EGR cooler seal degradation can cause coolant to mix with engine oil, risking catastrophic bearing failure.

mainEntity.name: Which Audi models use the CPMA engine code?

acceptedAnswer.text: The CPMA is widely fitted across mainstream Audi premium models from 2012 to 2018, most notably the A6 (C7), A7 (C7), and Q7 (4L/4M). It was a high-volume application designed to balance strong torque delivery with Euro 6 compliance. Always verify your specific fitment using your registration number before ordering parts.

mainEntity.name: Should I buy a used or reconditioned CPMA engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: A reconditioned Audi CPMA is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the known risks of inheriting timing chain and EGR cooler faults. Used engines carry a 3-6 month warranty and may have undocumented rear-chain stretch. Reconditioned units include revised tensioners, new EGR assemblies, and a 12-24 month warranty.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my car has the CPMA engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: The CPMA engine code is stamped on a machined pad on the engine block, near the transmission bell housing, and is listed on your V5C registration document. It is commonly confused with earlier 3.0 TDI codes like CDUC or later variants like CVMD. Fitting the wrong revision can cause ECU mapping mismatches and turbo plumbing incompatibilities.
